 ## Search results
Recent work supports improving negative selection and loss calibration before changing the BERT4Rec backbone. [Correcting the LogQ Correction (RecSys 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.09331) identifies a sampled-softmax bias: the positive is always included, whereas negatives are sampled. Its refined correction treats these contributions separately and introduces an uncertainty-dependent weight. This addresses sampling bias, not false-negative labels. [Improved Estimation of Ranks (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06371) corrects sampled rank estimates, enabling efficient WARP/LambdaRank optimization; relevant when considering ranking losses instead of softmax. Neither establishes gains on the four target Amazon categories.

Hardest-only mining risks emphasizing unobserved positives. [EMM (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026004090) reports a controlled hard–random mixture with ID exclusion and similarity-window filtering for contrastive recommendation. Its safeguards are transferable hypotheses, rather than validated BERT4Rec improvements. A practical experiment would retain masked-target training and appended-mask inference, compare uniform sampled softmax against a gradually introduced moderate-hard/random mixture, exclude known training positives and duplicate candidates, and cap or downweight extreme-hard negatives. If approximating full softmax, correction must match the actual proposal distribution; deterministic top-k mining cannot simply inherit uniform-sampling correction. Train these objectives within one BERT4Rec per category, with no inference fusion. Select using fixed macro validation HR@10 across all four categories; inspect Industrial_and_Scientific and Electronics separately, but do not infer improvement from larger training margins.

---

Recent results support content-aware and time-aware sequential modeling, but the search did not identify a verified 2024–2026 paper matching every constraint: BERT4Rec, jointly learned title/description features, timestamp-aware attention, and no pretrained weights. [Improving Sequential Recommendations with LLMs (2024; revised 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01339) reports gains from LLM-initialized BERT4Rec embeddings, which require prohibited pretrained representations. [DenseRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.18442) learns projections from pretrained content embeddings and reports improvements mainly from representing unseen history items; its experiments use SASRec, so it does not establish gains for the required architecture. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://dspace.hansung.ac.kr/bitstream/2024.oak/10390/2/AR_D2A1A2_ITS-Rec_%20A%20Sequential%20Recommendation%20Model%20Using%20Item%20Textual%20Information.pdf) combines textual features with sequential attention, but uses pretrained BERT and unavailable review text.

For temporal modeling, [TemProxRec (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09784) incorporates absolute/relative temporal and positional embeddings into attention, plus contrastive learning across interactions occurring near one another in time. It distinguishes short versus long interaction gaps and reports benchmark improvements. A constraint-compatible hypothesis—not a directly verified published recipe—is one BERT4Rec network combining item IDs with a small, randomly initialized token encoder over available titles/descriptions, trained jointly through masked-item prediction, plus bucketed time-gap attention biases. Retain reserved-mask training, appended-mask inference, and one checkpoint per category. Text and temporal additions need validation ablations: published gains involving pretrained semantics, external data, or different backbones do not establish improvement in this benchmark.

---

Random masking creates a real objective mismatch, but terminal masking is already part of the original BERT4Rec method: its authors explicitly include samples masking only the last item to improve alignment with next-item prediction. Inference appends a reserved [MASK] and scores from that token’s representation. Thus, increasing terminal-task exposure is a grounded experiment, although improved HR@10 under this benchmark remains unproven. [Original BERT4Rec, §3.6](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.06690).

Recency-based Sampling of Sequences (RecSys 2022) argues that arbitrary masked-item reconstruction is only weakly aligned with recommendation and samples recent targets more frequently while retaining nonzero probability for older targets. Its experiments concern other backbones, so adapting this sampling to BERT4Rec is a hypothesis, not an established BERT4Rec result. More recently, Masked History Learning (2025 preprint; revised 2026) transitions from history reconstruction toward inference-aligned next-item training, but studies generative recommendation rather than a direct BERT4Rec masking comparison. [Recency sampling](https://arxiv.org/html/2207.02643), [MHL](https://arxiv.org/html/2509.23649).

Practical single-model experiment: mix random Cloze batches with terminal-mask batches generated from training-only prefixes; optionally increase the terminal fraction late in training. Sample prefix endpoints with a tunable recency bias. For each terminal example, replace its target with [MASK] and exclude every later interaction, preserving bidirectional attention over the visible prefix.
